common_name: Canary Brilliants Itoh Peony (Yellow Intersectional Peony with Red Flares)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Canary Brilliants is an intersectional (Itoh) hybrid bearing semi-double, clear yellow flowers marked with bold red flares radiating from the center, a more strongly patterned bloom than the plainer yellow of Bartzella, held on strong, woody-based stems that need no staking even under the weight of the large flowers. Its clean, deeply cut foliage stays attractive through summer and into fall well after bloom finishes, and like other Itoh hybrids it tolerates more heat and a wider soil pH range than straight herbaceous peonies, performing into zone 9 with afternoon shade. The plant dies back to the ground each winter like an herbaceous peony rather than persisting as a woody shrub, so cut old stems back after they yellow in fall.

common_name: Kopper Kettle Itoh Peony (Copper-Orange Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Kopper Kettle produces large, semi-double flowers that open a warm copper-orange and shift through peachy tones as they age, one of the less common color breaks among Itoh hybrids and a striking companion to the more common yellows and pinks. Like other intersectional hybrids it combines the flower form and color range of tree peonies with the reliable die-back-to-the-ground habit and cold hardiness of herbaceous peonies, and its strong, self-supporting stems hold the heavy blooms upright without staking. Foliage stays deeply cut, glossy, and disease-resistant well past bloom, giving good structure in the border through summer. Divide only when necessary, since Itoh peonies resent disturbance and can take a couple of seasons to rebloom fully after moving.

common_name: Red Rocket Crape Myrtle (Fast-Growing Red-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Red Rocket is one of the fastest-growing red crape myrtles, reaching flowering size and full height quickly compared to older red cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun (at least 6 hours of direct sun for best flowering). Red Rocket was bred for exceptionally vigorous, fast growth combined with large, vivid true-red flower clusters that hold their color well without fading to pink in intense summer heat, a common weakness in older red crape myrtle cultivars. It reaches a substantial upright, vase-shaped form more quickly than most named cultivars, making it useful where a fast-establishing specimen or screen is wanted, and it shares the improved powdery mildew resistance bred into modern crape myrtle introductions. Never top or hard-prune the main framework, since this practice, sometimes called crape murder, permanently disfigures the tree's natural vase shape; instead prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing, damaged, or overly twiggy growth.

common_name: Pink Velour Crape Myrtle (Dark Purple-Leaved Pink-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Pink Velour holds dark burgundy-purple foliage color best with full sun exposure, fading toward green in shadier sites.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun for the deepest, most saturated foliage color. Pink Velour pairs dramatic, near-black burgundy-purple foliage that emerges nearly black in spring and matures to a deep wine-purple with rich rose-pink flower clusters through summer, a striking contrast that makes it a strong specimen or accent even before bloom. Its medium size fits smaller landscapes and foundation plantings better than the largest white crape myrtle cultivars, and it shares the good powdery mildew resistance of modern breeding programs. Prune selectively in late winter to remove crossing or twiggy growth and maintain an open form; avoid heavy topping, which destroys the natural vase shape and reduces next season's bloom.

common_name: Coral Magic Crape Myrtle (Color-Changing Coral-to-Orange Dwarf Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container plants in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Coral Magic is a compact, shrub-form crape myrtle whose flower color shifts from coral-orange to deeper red-orange as blooms age, giving a multi-toned display.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Coral Magic is part of a compact, shrub-sized series of crape myrtles bred for smaller landscapes, foundation plantings, and large containers, bearing clusters of vivid coral-orange flowers that deepen toward red-orange as they age, so a single truss shows several tones at once through the long summer bloom season. Its naturally rounded, dense habit needs little to no pruning to maintain shape, unlike full-size crape myrtles that are often disfigured by improper topping, and it shares the improved powdery mildew resistance of modern breeding. Water regularly the first season to establish a deep root system; established plants are drought-tolerant and need only occasional deep watering through summer.
